headline: Scribd confirms security incident, exposing user email, last 4 digits of credit cards
summary: An unauthorized third party gained access to user data, including email addresses and partial credit card information. Scribd states there is no evidence of data misuse.
details: Scribd, Inc., the parent company of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, has announced a security incident. An unauthorized third party accessed certain user data within one of its systems. The company detected the access and has since secured the affected system.

The compromised data includes user email addresses. Additionally, the last four digits of credit cards, country, issuer, expiry date, and payment history (excluding full credit card details) were accessed. Scribd emphasizes that there is currently no evidence that this data has been misused.

In response, Scribd has notified law enforcement and relevant data protection authorities. They are also working with a third-party cybersecurity firm to enhance access controls and monitoring. The company regrets the incident and any concern it may cause.

Users are advised to remain vigilant against phishing attempts. Scribd, Inc. will never ask for usernames, passwords, or sensitive information via email or text. If suspicious messages are received, users should type the website URL directly into their browser or contact Scribd's dedicated call center.

headline: Semiconductor market loses $1 trillion as Intel's stock plunges 30% in a single day
summary: Intel's shares plummeted 30% on Friday, wiping out nearly $150 billion in market cap and triggering a massive selloff across the industry.
details: The semiconductor industry saw approximately $1 trillion in market capitalization wiped out on Friday, following a disappointing financial outlook from Intel. This widespread decline was triggered by Intel's significant stock plunge.

Intel's shares crashed 30% on Friday, resulting in a loss of nearly $150 billion in market capitalization in a single day. This marks the largest single-day loss in the company's history, driven by an anticipated drop of over 20% in sales from its client computing group (CCPG).

The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index (SOX), tracking 30 major semiconductor companies, plunged 9.14% on Friday. While Intel was the biggest loser, other chip-related stocks like Arm (-12.68%), AMD (-12.48%), and Qualcomm (-12.14%) also suffered considerable losses. Nvidia, despite a smaller percentage drop of 5.66%, lost around $270 billion in absolute dollar terms, exceeding Intel's loss.

The downturn extended beyond chipmakers to server manufacturers and cloud giants, with Dell (-12.67%), HPE (-8.10%), and Oracle (-6.88%) seeing significant value drops. Investors are reportedly questioning the scale and sustainability of capital investments required for AI infrastructure expansion.

Intel's Client Computing and Physical AI Group (CCPG) generated $8.1 billion in revenue during Q3 2026, a 5% year-over-year and 9% sequential decline. Weaker demand and increased competition led to a 14% year-over-year reduction in client processor shipments, partially offset by a 9% increase in average selling prices. CCPG accounts for nearly half of Intel's revenue and is its main cash source.

Intel projects its Q4 revenue to be between $15 billion and $16 billion, anticipating further deterioration in the client market through Q4 2026 and into 2027. The company expects the client PC market to decline 10% in 2027 compared to 2026, impacting CCPG performance.

Despite expecting its data center business to grow in 2027, industry-wide supply constraints will limit Intel's ability to fully capitalize on demand. Intel's market capitalization has dropped by nearly 50% since mid-June, as investors recognized CCPG's heavy dependence on memory prices and customer sensitivity to overpriced systems.

Surprisingly, Apple (-1.66%), a major client product seller, was largely unaffected by Intel's client computing group performance. Investors likely view Apple as more resilient to memory price fluctuations, despite the company being the world's largest supplier of microprocessors when including its A-series SoCs.
